Young Man Builds Insane Chevy C10 Truck in His Driveway: V8 Punch and 600 Horsepower
21 photos
Photo: Autotopia LA | YouTube
Roman is 25, and he has spent the past few years working on his 1971 Chevrolet C10 right in his driveway and then racing it. The street-legal, ferocious autocross machine now hits the streets and the track, pushed forward by a completely rebuilt V8 engine, with the force of 600 horsepower.
Roman is less than half the age of his street and track companion that he rebuilt from the ground up. He did most part of the job right in his driveway, not a shop, not a garage , with no lift at hand, just jacks that made enough room for him to get underneath and work. He is definitely an old soul who treasures retro styling as much as he loves autocross.
It looks like, after 55 years on and off the road, the Chevy C10 finally got in the right hands. Those of a young man who knows exactly what it can do with a bit of a power bump. Or more than a bit. The first owner of the C10 was a farm truck guy who used it as a workhorse. The second owner bought it for his son. Roman bought it from him and slowly but surely turned it into a race truck.
He built it with purpose. Everything has a function, it’s not all show and no go. It’s got no AC, but comfort wasn't exactly a top priority for him. Instead, fun was. Loud was. Performance was. He didn't build it to take it to car shows and brag about it. He built it to take it to the track and win.
Photo: 1971 Chevrolet C10 A fully built 383-cubic-inch small-block V8 sits under the hood. Roman retained the original engine block. He originally planned to swap it for a 440, but changed his mind and just rebuilt the 383 and made it run on high-octane 101 race gas. A Tremec TKX five-speed transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels.
From farm workhorse to track machine Now it makes over 600 horsepower and 600 pound-feet of torque. A Black Widow exhaust , coming out through the side, roars out the drama of the V8 from under the hood. The power plant was outfitted with a high-performance FiTech EFI setup, which Roman credits for providing razor-sharp throttle response and reliable drivability whether he's cruising on the highway or carving corners at the track.
He is still considering an upgrade to the suspension , currently featuring Viking Performance components, but he has to come up with the right setup. A specialized Nine Lives Racing frame-mounted rear wing showed up at the back to add crucial downforce over the rear tires. A McLeod clutch helps him when he wants to smoke the tires. He was after fun and wanted a truck that he could beat on. He doesn’t want to have to baby the truck.
Photo: 1971 Chevrolet C10 The truck is sitting on a Currie 9-inch, which serves as the bulletproof backbone of this build. It effortlessly absorbs aggressive downshifts, hard clutch drops, and heavy corner-exit acceleration without flexing or breaking a sweat under track conditions. Roman relocated the fuel tank to the back for improved weight distribution.
Roman runs a high-performance Wilwood disc brake setup to safely and consistently slow his good, old 1971 Chevrolet C10 down during high-speed autocross runs or whenever he wants to show off on the highway.
Less is more when you're after fun The cabin is simple and focused on performance, because sometimes, less is more. The driver and passenger sit in RaceQuip fixed-back racing seats. It is not exactly the most comfortable sitting choice, but Roman chose them for the enhanced racing feel that he gets on board. He never wanted to build a lounge on wheels. Those seats make perfect sense in a truck that spends more time at the track than it does on the road.
The driver holds a Cannonball Performance steering wheel and gets all the relevant driving data on the aftermarket digital and LED Intellitronix gauge cluster, with a classic yet sporty appearance. That is what the truck's creator wanted in the first place.
Photo: 1971 Chevrolet C10 Roman retained the original door panels, along with the door hinges and window cranks, but came up with a Level 7 pedal assembly. Roman made efforts to keep the truck looking as vintage as possible so that he would not alter its DNA.
On the road, the driveway-built Chevy C10 is stiff, light, and bad-mannered when you step on it. It can smoke tires until tomorrow (and until it runs out of rubber, of course), and it can make other motorists scratch their heads in surprise at the stoplight.
Looking all beat-up and run-down, nobody would expect it to launch like a rocket. Roman hasn't fixed the paint imperfections and isn’t planning to do it. Told you he's an old soul and patina works for him.
